section.title: The Triumphal Entry and the Temple
section.sectionRationale: The long journey ends. Jesus rides into Jerusalem on a borrowed colt while the crowds spread their cloaks and hail Him as the King who comes in the name of the Lord, and when the Pharisees object, He says that if these were silent the very stones would cry out. Yet as He sees the city He weeps, for it did not recognize the time of its visitation and judgment is coming. Entering the temple, He drives out the sellers, declaring that God's house of prayer has been made a den of robbers, and He teaches there daily while the leaders plot His death.
section.thesis: Jesus comes to Jerusalem as her humble King, hailed with words He accepts as His due, yet He weeps over a city blind to her visitation and cleanses the temple as its Lord, so that the King's arrival brings both salvation offered and judgment warned.
section.frameNote: Three movements: the Triumphal Entry on the colt; Jesus weeping over Jerusalem; and the cleansing of the temple with the daily teaching that provokes the leaders.

units.label: The Triumphal Entry
units.note: Blessed is the King who comes in the name of the Lord

verses.text: After Jesus had said this, He went on ahead, going up to Jerusalem.
As He approached Bethphage and Bethany at the Mount of Olives, He sent out two of His disciples,
saying, “Go into the village ahead of you, and as you enter it, you will find a colt tied there, on which no one has ever sat. Untie it and bring it here.
If anyone asks, ‘Why are you untying it?’ tell him, ‘The Lord needs it.’”
So those who were sent went out and found it just as Jesus had told them.
As they were untying the colt, its owners asked, “Why are you untying the colt?”
“The Lord needs it,” they answered.
Then they led the colt to Jesus, threw their cloaks over it, and put Jesus on it.
As He rode along, the people spread their cloaks on the road.
And as He approached the descent from the Mount of Olives, the whole multitude of disciples began to praise God joyfully in a loud voice for all the miracles they had seen:
“Blessed is the {{basileus|King}} who comes in the name of the Lord!” “Peace in heaven and glory in the highest!”
But some of the Pharisees in the crowd said to Him, “Teacher, rebuke Your disciples!”
“I tell you,” He answered, “if they remain silent, the very stones will cry out.”

units.label: Jesus weeps over Jerusalem
units.note: you did not recognize the time of your visitation

verses.text: As Jesus approached Jerusalem and saw the city, He wept over it
and said, “If only you had known on this day what would bring you {{eirene|peace}}! But now it is hidden from your eyes.
For the days will come upon you when your enemies will barricade you and surround you and hem you in on every side.
They will level you to the ground, you and the children within your walls. They will not leave one stone on another, because you did not recognize the time of your {{episkope|visitation}} from God.”

units.label: The cleansing of the temple
units.note: My house will be a house of prayer

verses.text: Then Jesus entered the temple courts and began to drive out those who were selling there.
He declared to them, “It is written: ‘My house will be a house of {{proseuche|prayer}}.’ But you have made it ‘a den of robbers.’”
Jesus was teaching at the temple every day, but the chief priests, scribes, and leaders of the people were intent on killing Him.
Yet they could not find a way to do so, because all the people hung on His words.

basileus.gloss: King. Luke's crowd hails Jesus not merely as one who comes in the name of the Lord but as the King, drawing on Psalm 118 and Zechariah's promise of a king coming humble and riding on a colt. Jesus accepts the acclamation as His due, for He is entering His own royal city, though His throne will be a cross.

eirene.gloss: Peace, the wholeness of the Hebrew shalom. Jerusalem, whose very name echoes peace, did not know the things that make for peace on the day her King came to her. The peace He brings is not political freedom but reconciliation with God, offered and, tragically, refused.

episkope.gloss: Visitation, a coming to inspect, to help, or to judge. Jesus weeps because Jerusalem did not recognize the time of her visitation, the day God Himself drew near in His Son. To miss the visitation of grace is to be left to the visitation of judgment.

proseuche.gloss: Prayer. Quoting Isaiah, Jesus insists that God's house is to be a house of prayer, a place of meeting God for all peoples, but it had been turned into a den of robbers. As Lord of the temple He purges it, reclaiming it for its true purpose of communion with God.

basic.context: The long road to Jerusalem reaches its goal. Jesus sends two disciples to fetch a colt no one has ridden, and rides into the city as the crowds throw their cloaks on the road and praise God for all they have seen, crying, Blessed is the King who comes in the name of the Lord. When the Pharisees tell Him to silence the crowd, He says that if they were quiet the stones would cry out. But as the city comes into view, Jesus weeps, for Jerusalem did not know the things that make for peace and did not recognize the time of God's visitation; enemies will one day surround her and leave not one stone on another. Entering the temple, He drives out the sellers, declaring that God's house of prayer has been made a den of robbers, and He teaches there every day while the leaders look for a way to kill Him.
basic.hermeneutics: See the King arriving to claim His city, and hold together the joy and the grief. The entry is a deliberate, humble messianic claim that Jesus accepts. The tears and the temple cleansing reveal that His coming is a crisis: salvation for those who receive Him, judgment for a city and a worship that reject Him.
basic.originalLanguages: The crowd hails Jesus as basileus, King. He weeps because Jerusalem missed what makes for eirene, peace with God, failing to recognize her episkope, her visitation. And He cleanses the temple to restore it as a house of proseuche, prayer, rather than a den of robbers.
basic.typology: The King riding a colt fulfills Zechariah's prophecy of the humble king coming to Zion. The praise of Psalm 118, Blessed is He who comes, is claimed by Jesus. The cleansing of the temple enacts Malachi's promise that the Lord will suddenly come to His temple to purify worship, and points to Jesus as the true temple.
basic.christ: Jesus is the humble King who comes to His city on a borrowed colt, the Lord who needs it and receives it, and the One whose praise even stones would sing. He is God visiting His people in person, weeping over them like the Lord over Israel of old, and the Lord of the temple who purges His Father's house.
basic.god: God comes near in His Son to save, and His visitation demands recognition and welcome. He grieves over those who will not know their day of peace, yet His justice is real, and He is jealous for the purity of His house, which is meant for prayer and communion with all peoples.
basic.crossReferences: Zechariah 9 foretells the king coming humble on a colt. Psalm 118 supplies Blessed is He who comes in the name of the Lord. Isaiah 56 calls the temple a house of prayer for all nations. Malachi 3 promises the Lord suddenly coming to His temple.
basic.oneStory: The journey ends with the King entering His city, welcomed and yet rejected, hailed by disciples and wept over by their Lord. The story turns here toward the cross: the visitation of grace is offered, the temple is claimed, and a people who will not know their peace set themselves to kill the King who came to bring it.

context.literary:
Luke 19:28 opens with a verb of motion, He went on ahead, going up to Jerusalem, and the whole passage is written as an approach, in four stages, each closer to the city. First comes the errand for the colt, verses 29 to 34, in which Jesus speaks with the foreknowledge of a prophet and the authority of a king. Then comes the procession down the Mount of Olives, verses 35 to 40, with its praise, its objection and its reply. The third stage is the lament over the city, verses 41 to 44, and the fourth is the entry into the temple, verses 45 to 48. The pace slows each time, and the joy of the first scenes gives way to tears and then to action.

The two halves form a deliberate contrast. In the procession everyone is praising: the whole multitude of disciples rejoices in a loud voice. In the lament Jesus alone is weeping. The crowd sees miracles and sings, verse 37, while Jesus sees the city and what is coming, verse 41. Luke wants us to hold both. The King is truly acclaimed, but the acclaim does not know what it is acclaiming. The word peace in the crowd's song, verse 38, is answered by the peace that Jerusalem did not recognise, verse 42.

The scene at the temple is very short in Luke. Where Mark describes tables overturned and a ban on carrying goods, Luke gives one sentence of action and then the scriptural verdict, verses 45 to 46. The result is that Jesus' attention rests on the two quotations, and on the teaching that follows. Luke's emphasis falls on what the temple is for, a house of prayer, and on His daily teaching, verse 47, which fills the temple for the remainder of the week.

The passage also closes a long arc. Luke's journey section opened at 9:51 with Jesus setting His face to go to Jerusalem, and the crowds, the Pharisees, the lepers and the beggar have been met along the way. Now He arrives. The reader who has noted the earlier hints, 13:33 and 13:34 to 35, in which He said that a prophet cannot perish outside Jerusalem and that the city would not see Him again until it said Blessed is He who comes in the name of the Lord, finds both statements being fulfilled in the song of verse 38.
context.historical:
The setting is the approach to Passover, when the city's population swelled with pilgrims. The road from Jericho climbs to Bethany and Bethphage on the eastern slope of the Mount of Olives, and from there it crosses the ridge and descends into the Kidron valley before the climb to the temple mount. At the crest, verse 37, the city lies in full view across the valley, with the temple at its centre. The Mount of Olives itself carried associations with the coming of the LORD, Zechariah 14:4, and with the flight of David from Absalom, 2 Samuel 15:30, so that a procession from it had a double resonance, of a king coming and of a king in exile.

The colt that no one had ever sat on, verse 30, matters. Animals that had never been put to work were set apart for sacred use, Numbers 19:2 and 1 Samuel 6:7, and a king's riding animal could not be used by others, 1 Kings 1:33 to 34, where Solomon is set on David's mule and acclaimed. Jesus' claim, The Lord needs it, is the claim of royal requisition, and the owners accept it. Spreading cloaks on the road was the gesture used when Jehu was proclaimed king, 2 Kings 9:13, a spontaneous act of homage to a person recognised as ruler.

The Pharisees' protest is not necessarily hostile; they fear that the crowd's cries will bring down the Roman authorities, who watched Passover crowds for any sign of revolt. Jesus' reply about the stones is a proverb of the kind found in Habakkuk 2:11, where the stones of a wall cry out against injustice.

Jesus' words in verses 43 and 44 describe a siege with a ramp or palisade, a closing in on every side and a destruction of the city and its inhabitants. This is the language of Jeremiah and the prophets on the fall of Jerusalem in 586 BC, and it would be literally fulfilled in AD 70 when Titus's legions surrounded the city and the temple was burned. Luke, writing later, includes the saying as a prophecy of what had happened.

The temple courts were the largest area of the complex, and the outer court was where animals and the half-shekel for temple dues were sold and changed. Such trade was a convenience for pilgrims who came from far away, and it was a function of the temple's economy. Jesus' protest is not about commerce as such but about a place that was supposed to be set apart for prayer.
context.canonical:
The passage is dense with Old Testament quotation and allusion, and each one lights up a different part of the story. The colt and the King come from Zechariah 9:9, where the king arrives righteous and having salvation, humble and riding on a donkey, and the context is the removal of chariots and war horses and the proclamation of peace to the nations, Zechariah 9:10. Luke does not quote the text, although Matthew and John do, Matthew 21:5 and John 12:15, and its shape can be seen behind every detail.

The praise comes from Psalm 118:26, the great pilgrim psalm sung as worshippers climbed to the temple. The cheer Blessed is the one who comes in the name of the LORD is addressed there to the pilgrim; Luke adds the word King. The psalm continues in a verse that Jesus will soon quote against the leaders, The stone the builders rejected has become the cornerstone, Psalm 118:22, in Luke 20:17. The two halves of the same psalm are used on the two sides of Palm Sunday and the cross. The song of the angels at Jesus' birth, Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace, 2:14, is echoed and altered in verse 38: peace in heaven. Peace is declared in heaven, but on earth it is hidden.

The weeping over Jerusalem takes up a role of the prophets. Jeremiah wept for his people when the city fell, Jeremiah 9:1, and Jesus' lament in 13:34 to 35 had already set Him beside Jeremiah. The prediction of the stones being thrown down joins the warning of Micah 3:12, which the elders later remember, Jeremiah 26:18, and anticipates His own words in Luke 21:6 and 20 to 24. The word visitation recalls the Old Testament language of God coming to His people for blessing or for judgment, Genesis 50:24 and Jeremiah 6:15.

The temple saying brings together Isaiah 56:7, My house will be called a house of prayer, and Jeremiah 7:11, Has this house become a den of robbers? Jeremiah's temple sermon warned that the building would not protect people who oppressed the weak and trusted in its walls, and that God would do to it what He had done to Shiloh, Jeremiah 7:12 to 14. Malachi 3:1 promised that the Lord would suddenly come to His temple and purify the sons of Levi, and all four Gospels show Jesus doing that. The cleansed temple prepares for the claim that He Himself is a greater temple, John 2:19 to 21, and for the church as the place of God's dwelling, Ephesians 2:21 to 22.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Luke wants his readers to see the entry as a royal event whose meaning only Jesus fully understands. He records the praise in generous terms, because the praise is true: Jesus is the King who comes in the Lord's name. But Luke also wants us to feel the tragic gap between the crowd's song and the city's response, and he shows it through Jesus' tears. The gospel's earlier promises, of a Saviour, a throne and peace on earth, have not failed. They are arriving, and the sad truth is that many will not recognise them.

Luke is also concerned to explain how the destruction of Jerusalem and the temple fits God's purposes. Many in Luke's audience, perhaps writing after AD 70, would have wondered how the holy city could fall if the Messiah had come. The answer in verses 41 to 44 is that the fall was foreseen and was the consequence of failing to know the time of God's visitation. Jesus does not exult over the destruction but grieves over it, and Luke wants readers to take the warning and the grief together.

The temple scene serves a third purpose. By recording Jesus' claim over the temple and His daily teaching in it, Luke prepares for the last conflict. The leaders who are looking for a way to kill Him are the ones who control the temple, and what Jesus says there in the next chapters will bring things to a head. The reader is meant to understand that the King who has come to the city is also the Lord who has come to His temple and that He is the one who decides what the temple is for.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
This passage describes what Jesus did on one particular day, and almost all of it is not a pattern for us. We are not told to look for a colt, to throw cloaks on roads or to drive out sellers. The cleansing of the temple in particular is sometimes used to justify anger or forceful protest in the church, but Luke records only that Jesus drove out those who were selling, and he gives the reason, which is the temple's purpose as a house of prayer. Jesus acted with the authority of the Lord of the house, an authority that no one else holds.

What does carry over is the logic. First, the King deserves praise, and it is right to praise Him joyfully and in public for what we have seen of His work, as the disciples do in verse 37. Second, His tears teach us how to look at a city that does not know Him. We are called to weep and not to gloat when judgment is announced. Third, the temple's purpose passes to the church, which is now the place of God's presence, 1 Corinthians 3:16 to 17. Whatever turns the worship of God into a marketplace, or makes access to Him harder for those who come from outside, is the target of this passage. Prayer is the centre of the Christian assembly, 1 Timothy 2:1 to 4, and the church should be a place where it can be offered freely.

The prophecy about Jerusalem is a description of a historical event that has been fulfilled. It is not a pattern for predicting later events, and it should not be used as a pretext for hostility toward the Jewish people. Jesus speaks as a grieving Jew to the city that He loves.

debates.question: What kind of king does Jesus claim to be on this day?

views.label: The humble king of Zechariah
views.case: By riding a colt and not a warhorse, Jesus enacts the king who comes in peace, Zechariah 9:9 to 10, and redefines what kingship means. The crowd's praise is accepted, and its political hopes are quietly corrected. The tears in verse 41 show that He knows the people have not understood.

views.label: An open messianic claim
views.case: The staged fetching of the colt, the acceptance of the King title and the refusal to silence the crowd amount to a public declaration of messiahship in the capital at Passover. The leaders understand it as such and begin to look for a way to kill Him, verse 47.

debates.bearing: These views are not rivals. The act is a deliberate messianic claim, and the content of that claim is Zechariah's king of peace. That is why the entry is both a triumph and the beginning of the passion.

debates.question: To what does Jesus' prophecy of the city's destruction refer?

views.label: The Roman destruction in AD 70
views.case: Verses 43 and 44 describe a siege, a levelling of the city and the loss of its inhabitants. The language fits what Titus did in AD 70, and Luke 21:20 to 24 repeats the warning in more detail. Most interpreters take it as a fulfilled prophecy.

views.label: A pattern that finds its end in the last judgment
views.case: Some argue that the Jerusalem judgment is a foretaste of the final judgment, so that the same language reaches beyond AD 70 to the end. The fall of the city becomes a warning of what awaits all who do not recognise the time of God's visitation.

debates.bearing: On either view the reason is given in verse 44, and it is the same reason for both: the time of visitation was not recognised. The message to later readers is the same, that to refuse the visiting God is to choose judgment.

debates.question: Was the temple cleansing a protest against corrupt trade or against the temple system itself?

views.label: A cleansing of abuse
views.case: The phrase den of robbers suggests that the leaders had turned a place of worship into a place of profit. On this reading Jesus acts as a reformer, purifying the temple so that it can be what Isaiah 56:7 said it would be.

views.label: A prophetic sign of judgment
views.case: The quotation of Jeremiah 7:11 recalls a sermon that foretold the destruction of the temple. On this reading the cleansing is an acted warning that the temple's days are numbered, because the leaders have rejected the one it was built to meet.

debates.bearing: Luke places the lament over the city directly before the cleansing and the plot to kill Jesus directly after it. The two readings can be held together: the act is a cleansing that also declares the old order cannot stand unless it receives Him.

study.originalLanguages:
The central noun of the passage is basileus, king, in verse 38. The crowd's cry quotes Psalm 118:26 but inserts the word, so that Blessed is the one who comes becomes Blessed is the King who comes. It is spoken here by a crowd of disciples. The earlier hint is the angel's promise of a throne in 1:32 to 33, and the next time the word is used of Him it is on the lips of Pilate and in the inscription on the cross, 23:3 and 38. The title is thus carried from the triumph to the crucifixion.

In verse 30 the animal is a polos, which can mean a young animal of the horse or donkey family. Luke does not tell us that it was a donkey, though readers familiar with Zechariah would supply it, and he stresses that it was one on which no one had ever sat. The statement that it was untouched by work belongs to the language of consecration. The owners are told to answer that ho kyrios autou chreian echei, the Lord has need of it. The word kyrios is the title Luke uses throughout for Jesus, and its use here is probably intentional, a claim by Jesus to the right of a master over what is His.

The verb in verse 41 is eklausen, He wept aloud. John's account of Lazarus uses a different word, edakrysen, which describes shedding tears, John 11:35. The verb klaio here describes loud lamentation, the sort of mourning that was expressed in the sound of the voice. Jesus does not shed a quiet tear. He weeps aloud over a city that is still standing.

His lament in verse 42 uses the words ta pros eirenen, the things that make for peace. Eirene is the Greek rendering of the Hebrew shalom, a fullness of well-being with God and with others. The disciples sang peace in heaven, but the city missed the things that lead to peace on earth. The verb ekrybe, was hidden, is in the aorist passive: the meaning has been concealed, and the question is whether it is a judicial hiding or a simple result of the city's blindness. Luke's own statement in 18:34 that the meaning was hidden from the disciples uses a similar idea.

The word in verse 44 is episkope, visitation. It is a word for oversight, and in the Septuagint it often describes the day when God visits His people, whether to bless, as in Genesis 50:24 and Exodus 3:16, or to judge, as in Jeremiah 6:15 and 10:15. Luke has already used the verb for God's coming to redeem in Zechariah's song, 1:68 and 78, and in the people's cry in 7:16. So the sad charge is that the city failed to recognise a visit that had been promised for centuries.

Finally in verse 48 the crowd was exekremato auto akouon, literally hung on Him as they listened. The verb ekkremamai means to hang upon, as a child hangs on a parent. The leaders are looking for a way to kill Him, but the people hang on His words, and that is why they cannot yet touch Him.

typology.type: The king riding a colt, Luke 19:35 to 38
typology.fulfillment: Zechariah 9:9 promised a king who comes humble and having salvation, and 9:10 says he will cut off the chariot and the war horse and speak peace to the nations. Jesus is the king of the promise, and His choice of a colt is a deliberate reading of that text. The correspondence is deeper than the animal: the peace He brings is made through a cross, Colossians 1:20, and His rule is over all nations, Revelation 19:11 to 16, where the King returns on a white horse. The type falls short of the whole story because the entry is a coming for peace and the return will be a coming for judgment, and the colt marks the first.

typology.type: The stones that cry out and the stone that is rejected, Luke 19:40
typology.fulfillment: Habakkuk 2:11 pictures the stones of a wall crying out against injustice,. Jesus says creation itself will praise if the people are silenced, and in Luke 20:17 He will quote Psalm 118:22 about the stone that the builders rejected. The two stone images belong together: the rejected stone is the one whom the living stones praise, 1 Peter 2:4 to 5. The correspondence is that stones witness to God's works. It falls short as a precise type, since the saying in verse 40 is a vivid statement and not a prophecy about specific stones.

typology.type: The weeping prophet and the fallen city, Luke 19:41 to 44
typology.fulfillment: Jeremiah wept for Jerusalem as the Babylonian army approached, Jeremiah 9:1 and Lamentations 1:16, and he preached the destruction of the temple, Jeremiah 7. Jesus stands in that line and surpasses it: Jeremiah was a prophet who grieved for a judgment he announced, and Jesus is the Lord who comes in visitation and grieves for the same city. Hebrews 3:3 says He is worthy of greater glory than Moses, and He is also greater than Jeremiah, for He takes the judgment upon Himself in the end. The lament is incomplete without the cross, where the one who wept over the city dies outside its walls, Hebrews 13:12.

typology.type: The temple and its Lord, Luke 19:45 to 48
typology.fulfillment: The temple was the place where heaven and earth met, and Jesus enters it as its Lord. Malachi 3:1 promised that the Lord would suddenly come to His temple. In John 2:19 to 21 Jesus speaks of His own body as the temple that will be raised, and in Revelation 21:22 the new Jerusalem has no temple, for the Lord God and the Lamb are its temple. The correspondence shows a building giving way to a person and then to a people. The temple falls short as a final dwelling because it could be defiled and destroyed, whereas the body of Christ was raised and the church is built on it, Ephesians 2:20 to 22.

study.christ:
The passage leads to Christ at the level of His identity. In verse 38 He is called the King who comes in the name of the Lord, and He accepts the title. Throughout Luke the question of who He is has been left open: a prophet, the Christ, the Son of the Most High. On this day He allows a crowd to say it aloud and defends their right to do so against the Pharisees, saying that the stones would cry out if they were silent. The King is not a figure in a story about someone else. He is Jesus of Nazareth, riding down the Mount of Olives.

The kind of king is defined by the details. A colt that has never been ridden means a mount that belongs to Him by right, and the owners' acceptance that the Lord needs it is a sign that His authority is recognised even by strangers. But the animal is humble. Matthew and John tell us this fulfils Zechariah, and the prophet's picture is of a king whose victory is peace. Philippians 2:5 to 8 describes the same pattern, one who did not count equality with God a thing to grasp but humbled Himself to the point of death on a cross. The triumphal entry is the first act of that humbling, a coronation on the way to a cross.

Jesus' tears reveal the heart of the King. He weeps because He knows what the city does not, and because He loves it. This is the Jesus who earlier said, How often I wanted to gather your children together, as a hen gathers her chicks, Luke 13:34. Hebrews 4:15 says that we have a high priest who sympathises with our weaknesses. The Lord who wept at the tomb of Lazarus weeps over a city, and He does not stop short of going to the cross for it. He does not stand outside His people's sorrow and judgment. He enters it.

The temple scene shows Him as the Lord of the house. He quotes Scripture as the one who has the right to apply it, and He acts with a sovereign authority that no prophet before Him had. It is His house, as verse 46 says: My house will be a house of prayer. Within days He will say that the temple will be thrown down, 21:6, and within the same week the veil will be torn, 23:45. He is greater than the temple, Matthew 12:6, and the whole movement of the passage is the Lord arriving at His house and revealing that its time as the place of meeting is about to pass into Him.

The caution here is not to turn the entry into an allegory. The colt need not stand for the Gentiles or the cloaks for our works, as some preachers have said. What the passage gives is a clear connection to Zechariah, Psalm 118 and Malachi, and an unmistakable direction towards the cross. The one who is praised as King is also the one the leaders want dead, and Luke does not let us separate the two.
study.god:
The passage shows a God who keeps His word to the smallest detail. The colt is found as Jesus said it would be, verse 32, and the saying in the entry, the lament and the temple all fulfil Scripture and prophecy. Luke's reader learns that the God who spoke through Zechariah, the Psalms, Isaiah and Jeremiah is the God who is now acting, and that nothing is out of His control, not even the rejection that Jesus predicts. What looks like the drift of events is the ordered fulfilment of what He said.

God is also the one who visits. The word episkope in verse 44 belongs to the language of God coming among His people, and Luke has already begun his Gospel with Zechariah saying that the Lord God of Israel has visited and redeemed His people, 1:68. The scandal of Jerusalem's failure is that God came in person and was not recognised. This shows something about God's character: He is not distant. He arrives in the midst of a crowd on a borrowed colt, and He is easy to miss because He comes humbly.

The passage also holds together grief and justice. Jesus' tears are not the weeping of a defeated man but of the Lord who sees what refusing Him will cost. The same God who wants peace for the city pronounces its judgment, and neither feeling cancels the other. In the Old Testament God says, I take no pleasure in the death of the wicked, Ezekiel 33:11, and Hosea 11:8 shows His heart torn between judgment and compassion. Luke 19 is that heart in the flesh. God's judgments are never cold, and His tears do not make Him weak.

His holiness shows in the temple. The place where He had promised to put His name is meant to be a house of prayer, and He is jealous for its purpose. The cleansing is a sign that God cares how He is approached and who may approach. Isaiah's text, in its context, says that His house will be a house of prayer for all peoples, Isaiah 56:7, and the court in which the traders had set up was the place where the nations were to pray. God's concern for the outsider is part of His holiness.

For worship, the passage teaches us to praise God for His mighty works, as the disciples do, and to do it with joy. It also teaches us to look at our own city and church with His eyes. We may sing for the King's coming and at the same time need to weep for those who do not know what makes for peace. And it teaches us to keep the place of prayer as the centre of our life together. A people who see that God has visited them will want to meet Him, and the God who has visited will receive them.

crossReferences.note: The king who comes to Zion is righteous, having salvation, humble and riding on a donkey. He will remove the chariots and the war horses and speak peace to the nations. This is the pattern Jesus follows in choosing a colt, and the context shows that the peace He brings is for the world and not for Jerusalem alone. Luke does not quote it, but all the details point to it.

The pilgrim psalm opens the gates of righteousness, speaks of the rejected stone, and says Blessed is he who comes in the name of the LORD. The crowd of verse 38 is singing the psalm, and Jesus will turn the other half of it against the leaders in Luke 20:17. The two scenes should be read together, since the same psalm celebrates the arrival and foretells the rejection.

At His birth the angels sang glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace among men. At the descent from the Mount of Olives the disciples sing peace in heaven and glory in the highest. The shift from peace on earth to peace in heaven reflects the city's refusal, and it frames the whole Gospel with songs of peace that the earth has not yet received.

Jesus said He must go on His way because a prophet cannot perish outside Jerusalem, and He lamented the city that kills the prophets. He said it would not see Him again until it said Blessed is He who comes in the name of the Lord. In 19:38 the disciples say it, though not the city. The lament of 19:41 is the fulfilment of the earlier one.

Jeremiah stood at the temple gate and told the people not to trust in deceptive words, saying the temple of the LORD, the temple of the LORD. They had made it a den of robbers by oppression and idolatry, and God would do to it what He had done to Shiloh. Jesus' quotation of Jeremiah 7:11 in verse 46 draws the whole sermon into the scene, with its warning that God will not protect a building for the sake of those who defy Him.

The LORD says that foreigners who join themselves to Him will be brought to His holy mountain and made joyful in His house of prayer, for His house will be called a house of prayer for all peoples. Luke gives only the first half of the verse, but the whole passage shows what the traders were obstructing, which is the space where the nations were meant to come near.

The Lord whom you seek will suddenly come to His temple, and He will purify the sons of Levi. The cleansing of Luke 19:45 is the beginning of that coming, and it is the Lord Himself, not a deputy, who does it. The passage also warns that the day will be hard to endure, which matches the tears of verse 41.

A woe is spoken over those who build a house by unjust gain, and the stones of the wall will cry out. Jesus' saying about the stones draws on this image: if the people were silent, the very creation would testify. Luke 19:40 fits the prophet's picture of a world that cannot be silent when wrong is exposed and God is about to act.

David has Solomon set on the king's own mule, anointed and acclaimed, and the people follow with such a noise that the ground shakes. The scene stands behind the entry as a precedent for the royal ride into the city. The new King comes not by a palace plot but by a prophetic word and the people's joy, and He is greater than Solomon, Luke 11:31.

Jesus tells the disciples that the temple's stones will be thrown down and that Jerusalem will be surrounded by armies. This is the longer form of the lament in 19:43 to 44, and it shows that what He saw from the Mount of Olives was not a passing mood but a prophecy that He would later explain. It is also the text that instructs believers in what to do when it comes.

study.oneStory:
The scene on the Mount of Olives belongs to a story that began when God made a place to dwell with His people. In Eden He walked in the garden, and the human pair were at home in His presence. When they were driven out, the way back was guarded, and the rest of the Old Testament follows God's long work to dwell among His people again, in the tabernacle, in the temple, and in the promise that He would one day return in person. Ezekiel saw the glory of the LORD leave the temple and stand on the mountain east of the city, Ezekiel 11:23, and the prophets promised that it would come back, Ezekiel 43:1 to 5. When Jesus comes down the Mount of Olives toward the temple, the story of the departing and returning glory is in view.

The story is also about kingship. From the promise to David that his throne would be established for ever, 2 Samuel 7:12 to 16, to the prophets who spoke of a righteous branch, Jeremiah 23:5, Israel waited for a king who would bring justice and peace. The kings of Israel and Judah disappointed, and the exile ended the line on the throne. Luke 19 is the day on which the promised King enters the city. The cry of the crowd is the cry of the whole Old Testament hope, and the colt is Zechariah's King at last.

But the story is also about the rejection that God allows. Jesus weeps because the city does not know what makes for peace. Yet He goes on into the temple and teaches, and the passion follows. God does not abandon His plan when it is refused. He carries it through the refusal. The cross is the place where the King is enthroned and the peace is made, and Paul says that on it Christ made peace through the blood of His cross, Colossians 1:20. What looked like the end of the story is the means by which it advances.

The temple Jesus cleanses will be replaced. After the resurrection, the Spirit comes at Pentecost and makes the church the dwelling place of God, Acts 2 and Ephesians 2:22. The destruction of the old temple in AD 70 is not an accident of history but the close of the age of shadows. In the new creation John sees no temple in the city, for the Lord God Almighty and the Lamb are its temple, Revelation 21:22.

The song of the disciples on the hillside will be taken up by a far greater company. Revelation 5 and 19 picture all creation singing to the Lamb, and the King returns not on a colt but on a white horse. The promise of Luke 13:35 will be fulfilled in full, when every knee bows, Philippians 2:10 to 11, and the city that did not know the time of its visitation will be replaced by one that is entirely at peace, a new Jerusalem where God dwells with His people, Revelation 21:2 to 3.

quiz.q: How does Jesus enter Jerusalem, and what does the crowd cry?

options.text: On a colt, while the crowds spread their cloaks and hail Him as the King who comes in the name of the Lord.
options.note: Luke 19:35-38 shows the humble royal entry and the messianic acclamation.

options.text: Riding into the city as the people praise God for His miracles.
options.note: True, but it omits the specific hail of Him as King and the royal cloak-spreading.

options.text: On foot, quietly slipping into the city unnoticed.
options.note: The entry is public and royal, on a colt with loud praise, not a quiet arrival.

options.text: On a warhorse, leading an armed procession.
options.note: He comes on a colt, the humble king of Zechariah, not a military conqueror.

quiz.q: What does Jesus say when the Pharisees tell Him to silence the crowd?

options.text: That if the disciples were silent, the very stones would cry out.
options.note: Luke 19:40 affirms that His praise is so fitting creation itself would voice it.

options.text: That the praise of His disciples is entirely appropriate.
options.note: True, but it misses the vivid claim that even the stones would cry out.

options.text: That He would ask the crowd to quiet down a little.
options.note: He refuses to silence them, insisting the praise cannot be stopped.

options.text: That the Pharisees were right to object.
options.note: He rejects their objection outright.

quiz.q: Why does Jesus weep over Jerusalem?

options.text: Because the city did not know the things that make for peace or recognize the time of its visitation from God.
options.note: Luke 19:42-44 gives both the missed peace and the unrecognized visitation.

options.text: Because judgment and destruction were coming upon the city.
options.note: True, but the root cause He names is that they missed their day of peace and God's visitation.

options.text: Because the people did not welcome Him with enough enthusiasm.
options.note: The crowds did welcome Him; His grief is over the city's deeper blindness to its visitation.

options.text: Because He feared what the leaders would do to Him.
options.note: His tears are for the city's blindness and coming ruin, not for Himself.

quiz.q: What does Jesus do in the temple, and how does He explain it?

options.text: He drives out the sellers, saying God's house of prayer has been made a den of robbers.
options.note: Luke 19:45-46 records the cleansing and the quotation of Isaiah and Jeremiah.

options.text: He clears out those who were selling in the temple courts.
options.note: True, but it omits His words explaining that the house of prayer had become a den of robbers.

options.text: He rebukes the priests for their long prayers.
options.note: The issue is the corruption of the temple market, not the length of prayers.

options.text: He praises the temple commerce as good service to pilgrims.
options.note: The opposite: He condemns it and drives the sellers out.

quiz.q: What is the response of the leaders and the people to Jesus' daily teaching in the temple?

options.text: The leaders sought to kill Him, but could not, because all the people hung on His words.
options.note: Luke 19:47-48 sets the leaders' murderous intent against the people's rapt attention.

options.text: The leaders wanted Him dead but were held back for now.
options.note: True, but it omits why they were held back: the people were captivated by His teaching.

options.text: The people were indifferent to His teaching.
options.note: The opposite: they hung on His every word.

options.text: The leaders welcomed His teaching in the temple.
options.note: They were intent on killing Him, not welcoming Him.

questions: Jesus accepted worship as the King who comes in the name of the Lord. Do you truly treat Him as King, or only as a helpful teacher, and where does His reign meet resistance in you?
The King wept over a city that did not know its day of peace. Are there people or places you have given up on that still move the heart of Christ to tears?
Jerusalem missed the time of its visitation. How might God be drawing near to you right now in ways you could fail to recognize?
Jesus cleansed His Father's house so it would be a place of prayer. What has crowded out prayer and true worship in your own life, and what needs to be driven out?
The people hung on His words while the leaders plotted against Him. When His teaching cuts across your plans, do you lean in to listen or look for a way around Him?

translationNotes.note: The acclamation quotes Psalm 118:26 and adds 'Peace in heaven and glory in the highest', echoing the angels' song at Jesus' birth. Luke alone calls the coming one 'the King', making the messianic claim explicit.
The prophecy 'They will level you to the ground, you and the children within your walls' was fulfilled in the Roman siege and destruction of Jerusalem in AD 70.
Jesus combines Isaiah 56:7, 'My house will be a house of prayer', with Jeremiah 7:11, 'a den of robbers', condemning the corruption of temple worship and reclaiming the house for its true purpose.
